text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on April 9 in history:
1241 - Mongol horsemen under Batu Khan, grandson of Genghis Khan, defeated the Teutonic Knights at Liegnitz, Silesia.
1454 - The Italian states of Milan, Florence and Venice signed the Peace of Lodi, recognising each other's status.
1483 - Edward IV, king of England, died. He became leader of the Yorkists in 1460 and became king after defeating the Lancastrians at Mortimer's Cross in 1461.
1553 - French writer Francois Rabelais died.
1626 - Francis Bacon, Baron Verulam of Verulam, Viscount St Albans, English statesman and writer, died. During the reign of James I, he rose to become Lord Chancellor in 1618.
1649 - The Duke of Monmouth, who led a failed rebellion against James II, born as James Scott. The illegitimate son of Charles I, his bid for the crown ended in defeat at Sedgemoor.
1683 - Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, claimed a large area of the American interior for France, naming it Louisiana.

1806 - Isambard Kingdom Brunel, greatest British engineer of his age, born; he built the Clifton suspension bridge, designed the Great Western steamship and was the engineer appointed to construct the Great Western Railway.
1835 - Leopold II, King of the Belgians, born. Devoted to expansion abroad, he was responsible for exploitation of the Congo basin, annexed to Belgium in 1908.
1865 - The U.S. civil war ended when Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered to Union General Ulysses S. Grant at Appomattox.
1869 - The Hudson's Bay Company agreed to cede its territorial rights to Canada.
1872 - Leon Blum, French Socialist prime minister, born. In May 1936 he became the first socialist prime minister since 1870. He was interned in Germany during the Second World War.
1882 - Dante Gabriel Rossetti, British poet, painter and co-founder of the pre-Raphaelites, died.
1898 - Paul Robeson, American singer and actor, born.
1906 - Hugh Gaitskell, British politician, born. Chosen to succeed Clement Attlee as Labour Party leader in 1955, he lost the 1959 election to Harold Macmillan's Conservatives.
1906 - Antal Dorati, U.S. conductor, born in Hungary. He was the first conductor to record all of Haydn's symphonies.
1926 - Hugh Hefner, American publisher of Playboy magazine, born. He invested $10,000 in the new magazine, launched in December 1953 with the then unknown Marilyn Monroe posing nude.
1932 - Carl Perkins, early American rock and roller who originally recorded "Blue Suede Shoes", born.
1940 - Germany launched its invasion of Denmark and Norway in World War Two.
1942 - After four months of siege, U.S. and Filipino forces on the Bataan Peninsula in the Philippines surrendered to the Japanese.
1945 - Dietrich Bonhoeffer, German theologian and anti-Nazi was executed in Flossenburg concentration camp. He was arrested in 1943 for his involvement in a plot to assassinate Hitler.
1959 - Frank Lloyd Wright, influential American architect, died. His buildings include the earthquake-proof Imperial Hotel in Tokyo and the Guggenheim Mueseum of Art in New York.
1960 - South African Prime Minister Dr Hendrik Verwoerd wounded in assassination attempt.
1963 - Winston Churchill was proclaimed an honorary U.S. citizen at the White House.
1969 - The supersonic aircraft Concorde made its maiden flight, from Bristol to Fairford in England.
1970 - Paul McCartney sought a High Court writ to wind up the Beatles business partnership, effectively ending the group's career.
1974 - India, Pakistan and Bangladesh signed an accord on the return of prisoners of war.
1977 - The Spanish Communist Party was legalised after a 38-year ban.
1981 - In Northern Ireland, IRA hunger striker Robert (Bobby) Sands won a seat in the British parliament in the Fermanagh and South Tyrone by-election.
1990 - The Hungarian Democratic Forum swept to power in elections, after 40 years of communism.
1991 - Georgia declared its independence from the Soviet Union, the second republic to do so.
1995 - Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori won re-election with a resounding first-round victory.
1996 - Former Congressman Dan Rostenkowski, once one of America's most powerful lawmakers, pleaded guilty to two criminal charges in a deal with prosecutors that called for a 17-month prison term.
